item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'A Zionist framing of Palestinian history': Why a book on Palestine was pulled from its publisher
item.description:
'A Zionist framing of Palestinian history': Why a book on Palestine was pulled from its publisher

Submitted by Mounira Elsamra on Fri, 10/23/2026 - 20:38
Authors Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari say the publisher made 'inaccurate' unilateral changes to their manuscript, including descriptions of 7 October 2023
Jenan Matari, a Palestinian-American activist, sits for a photograph at Haraz Coffee in New Brunswick, New Jersey, on 15 September 2025 (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
Off

A book deal with Penguin Random House, the world's largest book publisher, was a dream for two Palestinian authors who had spent the last two years working on a book detailing Palestinian history.

Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari are both vocal Palestinian-American activists with sizable online audiences. For them, the deal with Penguin Random House was an opportunity to educate many young readers about Palestinian oppression. 

Matari, who also spoke on behalf of Hadid, told Middle East Eye they believed their work could impact young readers' perspectives on the Palestinian struggle for liberation from the illegal Israeli occupying force and give them tools to call out oppression.

The book was set to be titled Displacement and the Palestinian American Story, part of an ongoing series of non-fiction books for young teens.

"Kids will eventually learn to connect dots very easily... and they will learn how to voice their rejection of other people's oppression," Matari said. 

But that deal came to a halt when their publisher refused to budge on several edits made unilaterally to their book, which the authors never reviewed or approved. 

Matari described the editorial process to MEE as strenuous and unconventional, saying their book went through several rounds of internal and external edits, with the publisher's legal and public relations teams also weighing in. 

The author said their book was already on sale for pre-order when issues began to arise with their publisher.

 "We had never actually seen the full manuscript until we basically had to beg for it in June of 2026," with the book set to be published just three months later, Matari told MEE.

That's when they discovered several changes had been made to their manuscript.

"The actions of October 7th [2023] were a violation of international law," read a line in the introduction to a chapter, omitting any space to include Palestinians' right to resist against an illegal occupying force, according to international law.

The authors were shocked to find this line that dismissed the Palestinian right to resistance. They reviewed their emails and documents to double-check if anyone from the publishing house had sought their permission for its addition.

When they addressed the publisher about removing the line, the heads at Penguin Random House told them: "If we did not include this line, the entirety of the book would be invalidated." 

Under international law, occupied people have a right to armed resistance, but the publishers sought to frame that resistance as unlawful, the authors said.

MEE reached out to Penguin Random House for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

'Our concern is not accuracy'

Matari said it's not her place to condemn how occupied people resist oppression and that she and Hadid reject the idea that diaspora Palestinians should do so. 

"To believe that you have the power or ability to do so is so arrogant," Matari said.

Matari said they believe these changes to their book were a result of "internal pressure to accommodate a Zionist framing of Palestinian history". 

When they exchanged emails with leadership at Penguin Random House about the editorial disputes, the authors were told: "Our concern is not accuracy." 

"To hear that that's not a concern... is just unacceptable," Matari told MEE. 

Are we not allowed to say a genocide began on 7 October, too?
Read More »

The publisher's response was a turning point for the authors, who describe the publisher's edits as ones that "were only being made to protect Jewish feelings, versus protect Palestinian existence", Matari said. 

"That was when we knew we had to move on."

Hadid and Matari's book was meant to be part of a larger Race to Truth series, Penguin Random House's nonfiction collection of seven books narrating global history from the perspectives of marginalised communities, including African Americans and Indigenous peoples. 

Matari told MEE that Penguin Random House also pushed back against the authors' use of the word "Jewish" as a modifier throughout the book, including in references to Jewish gangs that carried out attacks against Palestinians before 1948. 

The authors had drawn on historical newspaper headlines, including from The New York Times and The London Times, that described the groups as "Jewish gangs" or "Jewish terrorists".

Matari said the publisher tried to make the terms "Jewish", "Zionist" and "Israeli" interchangeable, which she rejected as historically inaccurate. 

"That was something that I really rejected, mainly because it was incorrect, but also for the safety of the Jewish community," she told MEE. 

For the authors, accuracy and the safety of others trumped any pressure from publishers. 

"We understood that it made people uncomfortable to read this, but unfortunately, history and decolonial history are supposed to make you uncomfortable," she said.

 "We refused to switch that term out just to appease other people's comfort."

The authors have since been returned the rights to their book, and they are now moving forward with independent Palestinian publishing house Interlink Publishing. 

Pattern of censorship

This is not the first time Matari has been at the centre of a book-related controversy. Just last month, Matari was one of two authors to file a lawsuit against the Los Angeles Public Library over the cancelled Read Palestine Week book event. 

The cancellation came after a staff librarian wrote a letter to library leadership alleging the authors had antisemitic views and terrorist ties. Both authors are alleging discrimination and First Amendment speech violations. 

'It's a reminder to myself how important this work is'

- Jenan Matari, author

Last year Matari authored and published Everything Grows in Jiddo's Garden, a Palestinian children's book, but she said her book promotion event at a Montclair bookstore was cancelled following a campaign from Zionists who pressured the bookstore to call off the event. 

The pattern of censorship is unsurprising to Matari.

 "There's something about teaching children about the truth of Palestine that people are very uncomfortable with," she said.

For Matari and Hadid, the issue is bigger than their publishing deal; it's about who gets to write history, who gets to frame it, and the access one loses to mainstream institutions when one stands up for their values.

"I think the majority of people who are continuously censored would be very discouraged to continue. But I'm kind of amped up. I use it as fuel. It's a reminder to myself how important this work is," Matari said. 

"If it's making this many people mad, if it's making this many institutions mad and uncomfortable, then you must be doing something right."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Sudan decries Nusseibeh UN candidacy as ‘whitewashing' Emirati role in civil war
item.description:
Sudan decries Nusseibeh UN candidacy as ‘whitewashing' Emirati role in civil war

Submitted by Daniel Tester on Mon, 10/26/2026 - 19:18
Lana Nusseibeh's late entry to the race for the top spot has brought widespread criticism
UAE assistant minister for political affairs and envoy of the Minister of Foreign Affairs Lana Nusseibeh addresses the United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, on 27 September 2025 (Charly Triballeau/AFP)
Off

Top Sudanese diplomats at the United Nations have called on states to reject Lana Nusseibeh’s bid to become UN secretary general, accusing the Emirati foreign minister of “whitewashing” the UAE’s role in Sudan’s civil war. 

Nusseibeh has emerged as a frontrunner to lead the UN since her last-minute entry to the race on Wednesday, amid a stalemate at the Security Council, whose 15 members have so far been unable to agree on a successor to incumbent top diplomat Antonio Guterres.

Nusseibeh's candidacy has caused uproar over the UAE’s role in Sudan’s civil war, where it is widely accused of supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary whose mass killings UN investigators say bear the “hallmarks of genocide”.

The UAE denies involvement. 

In a statement given exclusively to Middle East Eye, Sudan’s permanent mission to the UN said it had “fundamental questions about Nusseibeh’s independence, impartiality and credibility” as a contender to hold the UN’s top job. 

“She has built her career on defending and whitewashing her country’s record of troubling the peace of Sudan by enabling genocide, the enslavement of our women and girls, sexual violence and other atrocities,” the office said.  

“The UAE must face accountability, not be rewarded with the top global leadership role of the UN.” 

The statement comes after MEE revealed that the UK is leaning towards backing Nusseibeh’s bid, according to numerous sources close to the British government. 

Denying Emirati involvement

Nusseibeh, who served as the UAE’s ambassador to the UN from 2013 to 2024 between stints in senior posts in the UAE’s foreign ministry, has long denied any Emirati involvement in the civil war. 

In April 2024, Nusseibeh told the UN Security Council that any allegations of Emirati support for the RSF were “spurious, unfounded, and lack[ing] any credible evidence”. 

'The UAE must face accountability, not to be rewarded with the top global leadership role of the UN'

- Sudan's permanent mission to the UN

When CNN asked in July 2024 whether she rejected UN investigators’ findings of “credible” evidence of Emirati support for the RSF, Nusseibeh said: “Absolutely”, adding that such allegations were “categorically untrue”.

Hundreds of thousands are estimated to have been killed since the outbreak of the conflict in April 2023, with millions more displaced. 

Nusseibeh travelled to Strasbourg in November 2025 to lobby the European Parliament to remove references to the UAE’s role in Sudan from an EU resolution condemning atrocities. Nusseibeh did not respond to MEE’s request for comment. 

As secretary general, Nusseibeh would be bound by the UN Charter to act independently of all governments, including Abu Dhabi. 

But Ammar Mahmoud, a top Sudanese diplomat at the UN, said her outright rejection of the UN investigators' findings on Emirati involvement signalled she would not undertake the role with due impartiality. 

“I highly doubt that she will ever form any investigative committees about the UAE’s role in Sudan,” Mahmoud told MEE.

“Nor do I think that she will accurately reflect, in her engagements with world leaders as secretary general, the true nature of the conflict in Sudan and her country’s role in it.”

Sudan accused the UAE of complicity in genocide in Sudan at the International Court of Justice in March 2025, but the case was dismissed two months later, as the UAE had not fully acceded to the Genocide Convention, meaning the court lacked the formal authority to rule on the matter. 

Israeli ties

Concerns have also been raised about Nusseibeh’s ability to mediate the Israel-Palestine conflict as secretary general, and her willingness to hold Israeli leaders to account for alleged war crimes in Gaza, where Israel has killed over 74,000 Palestinians since October 2023.

Exclusive: UK leans towards backing UAE's Lana Nusseibeh for UN secretary-general
Read More »

Although the UAE has repeatedly voted against Israel at the General Assembly, Abu Dhabi and Israel have had close ties since they signed the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020, a landmark deal championed by Nusseibeh that ended decades of diplomatic boycott. 

Last week, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave a security presentation outlining an “Israel-UAE Hexagon Alliance”, which also appeared to name Sudan’s RSF as a “friendly” party. 

If selected, Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage, would be the first woman to lead the UN and its second Arab secretary general, despite pressure for the next officeholder to come from Latin America, given conventions about regional rotation. 

Nusseibeh’s entry into the race last week followed six informal straw polls in which no candidate secured the required backing of all five veto-wielding permanent members of the Security Council: the UK, the US, Russia, China, and France.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'Shithouse countries': Trump has pledged not to use such language again, adviser says
item.description:
'Shithouse countries': Trump has pledged not to use such language again, adviser says

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Mon, 10/26/2026 - 15:53
The US president, campaigning for Republicans across the country, said he doesn't want immigrants from Libya, Yemen, and Somalia coming to US
US President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a midterm elections rally at McMorran Place Sports and Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Michigan, on 25 October 2026 (Alex Wong/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

After US President Donald Trump called a number of Arab nations "shithouse countries" on Saturday, his newly minted adviser on Arab-American affairs said the US president has since promised he wouldn't do it again. 

"Libya, Yemen, Haiti, Somalia. Remember what I called them? Shithouse countries," Trump told a crowd of supporters at a rally in Perry, Georgia, where he is drumming up support for Republican candidates ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

He added that the countries are "terror-infested".

"Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from like, well, Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?"

Amer Ghalib, his Yemeni-born adviser, wrote on his Facebook page on Sunday that he "contacted the president via text message" to express his "dismay and rejection of those remarks".

He said he later met with the president ahead of his rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, and "reiterated my request".

"He expressed understanding of the situation and pledged to address the issue and ensure it does not recur," Ghalib added. 

The Facebook post was in Arabic only, whereas Ghalib normally provides an English translation as well. 

At his rally in Michigan, Trump did not go after Arab and Muslim countries, but did very much go after the surging Arab and Muslim Democratic candidate for Senate in the state, Abdul El-Sayed. 

'I think this language is indicative to me as a language of desperation'

-Bishara Bahbah, founder, Arab Americans for Trump

“I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump told the crowd.

Sayed, he added, "wants our country to go to Sharia law, and if he ever pulls that off, he should be the first one that’s tried. I’ll be a witness". 

There are no known links between Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood, an ideological political party largely suppressed in the Middle East. Three of its offshoots were designated as terror organisations by the US president last year. It has no central hub. 

"I think this language is indicative to me as a language of desperation," Bishara Bahbah, the Palestinian American former Harvard academic who founded "Arab Americans for Trump" in 2024, told Middle East Eye on Monday. 

"It's very different than the Trump we knew in 2024, when he was very careful not to offend anybody, and he was very careful to thank the Arab and Muslims for their vote. Now, the stakes for the president are not the same."

In a written statement shared with MEE, Jenin Younes, the president and legal director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, said the rhetoric at Trump's rallies "is tired, dangerous, and designed to distract from the realities facing everyday Americans".

"I hope voters see through these tactics so we can come together and focus on getting this country back on track."

'Red line'

The president has seemed mostly unbothered by the potential outcome of the midterms, even as analysts predict a blue wave that could mean the House and Senate go to the Democrats.

So much so that he's choosing to campaign in red Republican districts - his comfort zone among supporters - rather than try to win over voters in other areas. 

Last week he told reporters at the White House that when he doesn't run, "people don't show up to vote", so he's asking them to "pretend I'm on the ballot". 

Abdul El-Sayed confronts heckler linking him to Muslim Brotherhood
Read More »

The midterms are very much a referendum on the conduct of the commander-in-chief. 

A Democratic victory would impede Trump's agenda for his final two years in office, and potentially lead to the impeachment of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth for the way the war on Iran has been handled. 

Trump's approval rating among Americans this month has hovered between 34 percent at its lowest, and 40 percent at its highest. 

The results stem from high fuel prices during an affordability crisis in the US, as well as tens of thousands of families being impacted by the sometimes violent mass arrests and deportations of immigrants. 

He also recently endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the 27 October election, despite deep disdain for Netanyahu among conservatives who have become critical of the US-Israel relationship. 

So is it still worth it for impacted communities to engage with this administration if the president's behaviour is so unpredictable and the power dynamic in Washington is about to undergo a dramatic shift?

Bahbah, whose goal in 2024 was to get Trump to end Israel's genocide in Gaza, told MEE he has been "rebuffed" by the White House in recent weeks, despite being a critical backchannel between US negotiators and Hamas in the lead-up to the 10 October 2025 Gaza ceasefire deal. 

Asked how that made him feel, he responded: "Like shit."

He said he has not been surprised by Trump's remarks towards Arabs and Muslims, but that it "crosses a red line".

"The president has been calling Chuck Schumer a Palestinian," Bahbah said of the top Democrat in the Senate. "We've spoken with the president and told him a Palestinian is not a slur, and not to use it, and he committed not to use it, and yet he uses it again," Bahbah said. 

In Michigan on Sunday, Trump praised his daughter's father-in-law, Lebanese-born Massad Boulos, for helping him win the Arab-American vote in Michigan two years ago. 

"My senior advisor for Arab and African affairs... he is unbelievable," Trump said. 

MEE was unable to reach Boulos by phone on Monday. 

Obama rallies with Sayed

Longtime conservatives within the Arab and Muslim community are particularly stung by Trump's - and, by extension, the Republican Party's - spate of offensive language, Omar Shajrah, former legal counsel to the Michigan House, told MEE on Monday.

"They stuck their neck out" for the president in 2024, he said. 

"The Yemeni community, they kind of label themselves as the more conservative of the Muslim community, right? Because of their traditions and their values. So I think it's hurt a lot of people... it's kind of hard to come back from."

Shajrah, who typically votes Republican, said he will not back Sayed's opponent, the Trump-endorsed Mike Rogers, even though he has supported Rogers in previous races. 

"They're doing a horrible job of communicating" their actual policies, he said of the GOP. 

Shajrah did not, however, vote for Sayed during Michigan's early voting, he told MEE. 

"I think Abdul is a great political athlete. I think he's very talented... he's a breath of fresh air for a lot of people."

While Trump made his "shithouse" remarks in Georgia on Saturday, former President Barack Obama - whom Trump repeatedly calls "Barack Hussein Obama" to emphasise his father's Muslim roots - joined Sayed for a rally in Detroit, Michigan. 

While in no way a progressive Democrat like Sayed, Obama is still seen as a kingmaker among establishment Democrats, and remains very popular in the Black community.

Abdul El-Sayed is under fire for joining forces with Obama in upcoming rally
Read More »

Michigan is largely a working-class manufacturing hub and a swing state at election time, so it could go either way. A win for Sayed would not just mean the country's first-ever Muslim in the Senate, but also that socialist-style ideas do indeed have a wide appeal. 

"We have seen this movie before," Obama told the crowd. "I starred in it. I've got a long-form birth certificate to prove it. This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."

The former president was referring to the birther controversy started by Trump in 2011, ahead of Obama's second re-election campaign. Trump, then a real estate mogul and reality TV star, claimed Obama was not born in the US, and drummed up so much frenzy in the media that Obama was forced to produce his birth certificate from Hawaii. 

That move by Trump was widely seen as the launchpad for his presidential campaign in 2015, as he played on the fears of many conservatives throughout the administration of the country's first Black president. 

"Abdul will always stand up to special interests to lower costs for Michigan families. He'll fight for you every day of the week," Obama said on Friday. 

"And by the way, imagine - because you already got a pretty good senator right here - imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa," he added, referring to former CIA analyst and the other Democratic senator from Michigan, Elissa Slotkin.

"You got a Muslim man. You got a Jewish woman - fighting for you in the United States Senate. That's something, Michigan, you can be proud of."

After US President Donald Trump called a number of Arab nations "shithouse countries" on Saturday, his newly minted adviser on Arab-American affairs said the US president has since promised he wouldn't do it again. 

"Libya, Yemen, Haiti, Somalia. Remember what I called them? Shithouse countries," Trump told a crowd of supporters at a rally in Perry, Georgia, where he is drumming up support for Republican candidates ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

He added that the countries are "terror-infested".

"Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from like, well, Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?"

Amer Ghalib, his Yemeni-born adviser, wrote on his Facebook page on Sunday that he "contacted the president via text message" to express his "dismay and rejection of those remarks".

He said he later met with the president ahead of his rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, and "reiterated my request".

"He expressed understanding of the situation and pledged to address the issue and ensure it does not recur," Ghalib added.
